entities.name: Cabinet of Japan
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cabinet of Japan (Naikaku) is the executive organ of the Japanese government, composed of the Prime Minister and up to 20 ministers of state. Established by the Cabinet Law of 1947 under the post-WWII constitution, the Cabinet holds executive power collectively and is responsible to the National Diet (legislature), creating Japan's parliamentary system of government.

Japan's modern cabinet system was established in 1885 during the Meiji Era under Itō Hirobumi, Japan's first Prime Minister, who modeled it on European cabinet governments particularly the Prussian system. The 1947 post-WWII constitution, written under US occupation, transformed the Emperor from sovereign to constitutional monarch, making the Cabinet the real executive power responsible to the elected Diet rather than the Emperor.

The Cabinet system has been dominated by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) almost continuously since 1955, creating the world's most durable single-party democratic rule. Japan has had over 100 prime ministers, with frequent leadership changes creating political instability (average PM tenure less than 2 years). Abe Shinzō became Japan's longest-serving PM (2012-2020), implementing 'Abenomics' economic reform. The Cabinet's constitutional constraints on military force under Article 9 have been incrementally reinterpreted to allow greater Japan Self-Defense Forces roles.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Japan's Cabinet system transformed the world's only country to experience nuclear warfare into a stable parliamentary democracy and economic powerhouse, while its Article 9 pacifism became a unique experiment in constitutionally renouncing war.
